title: Cramming for success: study and academic work
subtitle: cram, revision, plagiarism, dissertation
summary: Talk precisely about studying, exams and academic writing, from cramming and rote-learning to deadlines, plagiarism and peer-reviewed papers.

lesson.heading: Study and exams
lesson.text: Before an exam, some students **cram** for it - they study in a very concentrated way for a short time. Even a **genius** (an exceptionally clever person) has to do some **revision**. If the exam comes round every year, you can revise by looking at **past papers**, the exam papers from previous years.

examples.text: I **crammed** all weekend and still ran out of time in the exam.
How much **revision** have you done for tomorrow's maths exam?
The best preparation is working through half a dozen **past papers**.

lesson.heading: Learning by heart, and beyond
lesson.text: Some things can be **memorised** or **learnt (off) by heart**. But **rote-learning** - learning purely by repetition - is not enough for most subjects. You can also use **mnemonics**: tricks that help you remember something. All things considered, the best idea is to **bury yourself in your books** and study **intensively** until you **know the subject inside out**.

examples.text: She learnt the whole periodic table **off by heart**.
'i before e except after c' is a **mnemonic** for English spelling.
Caspar is bound to do well in mechanics - he **knows the subject inside out**.
For the last fortnight he has **buried himself in his books** and studied **intensively**.

lesson.heading: Kinds of written work
rows: just 50-100 words, often used for school work
longer and more serious than a composition; hundreds or thousands of words
a long essay, often part of a course, usually thousands of words
like an assignment, but the emphasis is on the student's own material and topic
a collection of individual pieces of work, which may include drawings and other creative work
a long, research-based work, perhaps 10,000-15,000 words, for a degree or diploma
a very long, original, research-based work, perhaps 80,000-100,000 words, for a higher degree such as a PhD

lesson.heading: Writing an essay
lesson.text: It is a good idea to start with a **mind map**, a diagram that lays out your ideas and how they connect. Always write a **first draft** - a first, rough version - before you **write up** the final one. Your essay must be all your own work: **plagiarism**, using other people's work as if it were yours, is a very serious offence.

examples.text: **Plagiarism** is an increasing problem because it is so easy to cut and paste from the internet.
Don't forget to sign the **plagiarism form** and hand it in with your dissertation.
If you quote an article, you must **acknowledge** your source, giving the author and title.

lesson.heading: Deadlines, submitting and feedback
lesson.text: There is usually a **deadline** - the date by which you must hand the work in. After the essay is **submitted** (the formal word for handed in), it will be **assessed**, that is evaluated and given a grade, and usually you can get **feedback**, the teacher's or tutor's comments.

examples.text: The **deadline** for the second assignment is midnight on Friday.
All coursework must be **submitted** electronically and will be **assessed** by two markers.
The **feedback** on my first draft was blunt but extremely useful.

lesson.heading: Higher academic study
lesson.text: University academics **carry out research** - less formally, **do research** - and are expected to read academic **journals**, which publish **papers** or **articles** on specialised subjects. If your library has no copy, you may be able to **access** it online or get it through an **inter-library loan**, the system where libraries exchange books and journals with one another.

examples.text: Orla has had a **paper** published in the British Medical Journal.
All students need a username and password to **access** journals online.
**Open educational resources** are online materials that teachers and students anywhere can use freely.

lesson.note: We do not call an academic journal a magazine.

lesson.heading: Surviving the course
lesson.text: Academic study can be very **demanding**, and some students **drop out** - leave the course before the end. The majority, though, survive until **finals**, the last exams of a college or university course, and become **well-qualified** members of their profession.

examples.text: Nearly a fifth of the first-year intake **dropped out** before Christmas.
She revised solidly for six weeks before her **finals**.
Some people take a long time to find suitable work even though they are very **well-qualified**.

lesson.text: Cram is short and intense; revise is steady and repeated - you cram the night before, but you revise for weeks.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of written work with its description.

pairs.right: a collection of several separate pieces of work
research-based, about 12,000 words, for an MSc
the student chooses the topic and does the research

exercises.prompt: His PhD ___ was 90,000 words long and was on the history of US place names.
exercises.explanation: A thesis is a very long, original, research-based work for a higher degree such as a PhD.

exercises.prompt: Little Martha did her first ___ in school today. It was called 'My family'.
exercises.explanation: A composition is a short piece, often just 50-100 words, used for school work.

exercises.prompt: I think I'll do a study of people's personal banking habits for my MSc ___. It has to be about 12,000 words.
exercises.explanation: A dissertation is a research-based work of around 10,000-15,000 words for a degree or diploma.

exercises.prompt: We have to hand in a ___ at the end of the course. It can consist of up to five different pieces of work.
exercises.explanation: A portfolio is a collection of individual pieces of work, which may include drawings and other creative material.

exercises.prompt: When I'm studying ___ because I'm cramming for an exam, I don't look at past papers.
exercises.explanation: To study intensively is to study in a very focused way.

exercises.prompt: There's no point in just learning things off by ___.
exercises.explanation: To learn something (off) by heart is to memorise it word for word.

exercises.prompt: It's a good idea to have some sort of ___ to organise your thoughts before you write.
exercises.explanation: A mind map lays out ideas for a topic and shows how they connect.

exercises.prompt: At the end of the day, you just have to bury yourself in your books until you know the subject ___ out.
exercises.explanation: To know something inside out is to know it completely.

exercises.prompt: What do we call the first attempt at writing an essay?
exercises.explanation: A first draft is the first, rough version, written before you write up the final one.

exercises.prompt: Which pair gives the more formal words for 'to hand in' and 'to mark'?
exercises.explanation: Work is submitted, then assessed - evaluated and given a grade.

exercises.prompt: What is the more formal way of saying 'do research'?
exercises.explanation: Academics carry out research; do research is the less formal version.

exercises.statement: If a student drops out, they leave the course before the end.
exercises.explanation: Correct - academic study is demanding and some students drop out before finals.

exercises.statement: An academic journal can also be called an academic magazine.
exercises.explanation: We do not use the word magazine for this kind of academic publication - it is a journal.

exercises.prompt: Does each word belong to exams and memorising, or to written work and research?
Put this piece of study advice in order.
exercises.answer: The best idea is to bury yourself in your books
exercises.explanation: To bury yourself in your books is to spend the maximum possible time studying.
